newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean premier Frei, Li Peng hold trade talks.
newsitem.headline: Chilean premier Frei, Li Peng hold trade talks.

text.p: Chinese Premier Li Peng held talks with Chilean President Eduardo Frei on Wednesday aimed at boosting trade ties and promoting Chinese investment in Chile's booming copper mining industry.

"China is interested in taking an active role in the copper business in Chile," said Frei at a news conference with Li. "We have studied various alternatives which will now be reviewed by mining authorities."
Li, the first Chinese leader to visit Chile, arrived in Santiago on Wednesday on the first stop of a Latin American tour that will include visits to Brazil and Venezuela.
His visit follows tours of the region earlier this year by Japanese leader Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean premier Kim Young-sam.
Chile, the world's largest copper producer, wants China to invest in building new copper mines, which would guarantee copper supplies for its own fast-growing domestic needs, said Frei.
Chinese mining officials will hold talks on Thursday with Chile's state copper giant Codelco and the private sector National Mining Society, he said.
Although trade between the two countries has risen sharply this decade, there is still room for improvement, Frei said.
"Trade figures show there is great opportunity for growth," Frei said.
Chile expects bilateral trade to total around $1 billion this year, compared with a scant $87 million in 1990.
Li said China -- struggling to feed its 1.2 billion people -- was also interested in increasing fresh fruit and agricultural imports from Chile.
Chile has recently been declared free of foot and mouth disease and eradicated the Mediterranean fruit fly, potentially clearing the way for millions of dollars of fruit and meat exports to Asia.

The two leaders signed three agreements including one on space cooperation, another on agriculture and a third allowing Chile to maintain its consulate in Hong Kong after the British colony is handed back to Beijing in July.
Li brushed aside questions on international criticism of China's human rights record, saying China did not accept foreign interference in domestic issues.
"The human rights situation has been improving and we are prepared to talk about it with anyone, but we do not accept interference in our internal affairs under the excuse of human rights," said Li.
Li leaves on Thursday for Brazil and travels to Venezuela next week.
